extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature — scientists, engineers, and academic professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing statistical analyses in astronomical studies (especially relationships between parallax and magnitude), as discussed in a critical correspondence and related review material on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of correlation measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the suitable statistical measure for the relationship observed — e.g., correlation coefficient vs correlation ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miss Gibson calculated the correlation coefficient between magnitude and parallax, between parallax and amount of light, plotted the regression line, and calculated the correlation ratio; finding a correlation ratio of 0.4 she concluded the correlation coefficient was not a suitable measure. Be aware that a non-linear (e.g., logarithmic) relation may make the ordinary correlation coefficient inappropriate and that the correlation ratio or transformation might better reflect association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for possible logarithmic relationships / transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the relationship between quantities (e.g., parallax and magnitude) is logarithmic rather than linear, and choose analysis accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Hinks suggested that if stars were uniform in size/brilliancy a parallax–magnitude relation would be logarithmic; reviewers note Miss Gibson was aware of and cited the possibility of logarithmic relationships. Analysts should test transformations and not rely on a single linear measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot regression and compute multiple association measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t rely on a single summary statistic; plot regression lines and compute complementary measures (coefficients, ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miss Gibson combined correlation coefficients with regression plots and the correlation ratio to assess the relation — an example of cross-checking measures and visual inspection to detect inadequacy of single statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware and test for selection bias in samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether the sample was selected on characteristics (e.g., proper motion) that could bias observed relationships between the variables of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Hinks argued peaks in the magnitude–parallax curve arise from selection by proper motion. The counterargument: for selection to strongly distort correlation between A and B, the selection variable must be highly correlated with both A and B. Explicitly assess selection mechanisms and their correlations with measured variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate hypothesised relationships statistically, do not assume them
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses such as 'brighter stars are closer' require statistical demonstration rather than axiomatic acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer emphasises that hypotheses of a high relation between magnitude and parallax (or proper motion) deserve proof; reviewers should demand empirical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative explanatory variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether other variables (e.g., spectral class, colour, mass, chemical constitution, stellar life-history) better explain observed variation than the hypothesised variable (e.g., distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes spectral class–magnitude correlations can be as high as 0.69 and colour–magnitude are at least as close as parallax–magnitude; reviewers should compare candidate predictors to identify stronger explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sufficiently large and representative samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ sample sizes and sets representative enough to avoid artifacts from small or atypical datasets (e.g., comparing Newcomb's 72 stars to Yale's 163 stars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites differing results between series of 72 and 163 stars, indicating increased sample size/coverage can reduce spurious correlations; reviewers should check sensitivity to sample size and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine measurement errors and their distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how measurement errors (e.g., large negative parallaxes, greater parallax errors for faint stars) affect observed relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer points out that descending magnitude with parallax groups may be due to large errors of parallax being more common with faint stars — so account for heteroscedasticity and error structure in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical logic about selection effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and apply statistical logic: selection on a characteristic only substantially alters correlation between two variables if the selector is highly correlated with both variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondence explicates the logical condition for selection-induced effects, advising reviewers to quantify correlations between selector and each variable before attributing biases to selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and comparability of figures and sections in technical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure figures (sections of dams/reservoirs etc.) are drawn to comparable scales and presented so they can be readily compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the irrigation book review the reviewer criticises reservoir-dam sections drawn to various scales as 'not readily compared' — technical publications should use consistent/scalable figures and note scales clearly to facilitate assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author expertise and relevance of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the author's practical experience and domain exposure (e.g., experience in India and Egypt for an irrigation book) as part of evaluating authority and suitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The irrigation book is praised because the author 'has gained his experience in both these countries' and draws examples from both — reviewers should weigh firsthand experience and contextual knowledge when judging technical works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative real-world examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the work uses relevant, large-scale or representative examples (e.g., Nile, Indus, Tigris/Euphrates) to illustrate principles and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer values the use of large-scale irrigation works from Egypt and India to present modern aspects; practical texts should ground principles in real projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of practicability and feasibility of proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge proposed engineering or policy schemes for practicality and likely success (e.g., rejecting a second dam higher up the Nile as impracticable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes some proposals are impracticable and others likely to silt up; critical evaluation should include feasibility, long-term performance, and hidden drawbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of implementation resources and funding
rubrics_metrics.description: For policy recommendations (e.g., plague prevention), evaluate whether adequate funding and resources are planned to carry out recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary points out government edicts give recommendations but say nothing about finding the money — reviewers and policymakers should require implementation plans and budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance public health measures against social resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: When recommending sanitary actions, consider social acceptability and the risk that insisting on avoiding public opposition may prevent necessary large-scale operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece warns that injunctions to 'avoid any action which excites the opposition of the people' could lead to abandonment of large-scale plague control; evaluation should weigh effectiveness versus sociopolitical constraints and consider communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of field expeditions and in-area research for tropical diseases
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the importance of carrying out research in the endemic area and of expeditions for discovery and practical outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review praises expeditions of the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine for yielding major discoveries and training; for tropical-disease research, in-field studies and expeditions are judged highly valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of laboratory and post-expedition research facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that material collected during fieldwork can be followed up and worked out in adequate research laboratories and that institutions create such facilities when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes the accumulation of material necessitated establishing a research department where parasites and animals can be maintained and experiments carried out — reviewers should check institutional capacity to complete research cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and dissemination of research outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the mode of publication and dissemination makes results widely available (e.g., changing memoirs into a broader journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises the change to the 'Annals of Tropical Medicine and Parasitology' to admit publications from others — consider reach, cost, and openness of publication venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and procedural requirements for academic appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: For hiring/appointment adverts: required academic qualifications, relevant laboratory and teaching experience, testimonials, use of official application forms, deadlines, and rules against canvassing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Job notices specify 'Honours Degree in Chemistry', laboratory experience, 'experience in technical work and class teaching desirable', submission on official form, 'copies of three testimonials', stamped addressed envelope for postal applicants, and that canvassing is disqualifying — these are explicit procedural and qualification criteria to be met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit application material limits and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications should comply with limits (e.g., not more than three recent testimonials) and be submitted by stated deadlines to specified offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Head of Art Department applications: 'accompanied by copies of not more than three recent testimonials' and 'should be received not later than Monday, September 23' — administrative compliance is a criterion for consideration.
